title: nmap — Scanning Your Network
objective: Learn how to use nmap to discover devices on your own home network and understand what open, closed, and filtered ports mean.
legalWarning: Only scan networks and devices you own. Scanning others' networks without permission is illegal under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (US), Computer Misuse Act (UK), and similar laws worldwide. Penalties include fines and prison.
explanation:
Imagine you just moved into a new house and you want to know what's inside every room. That's basically what nmap (Network Mapper) does — it looks around your network and tells you what devices are connected and what 'doors' (ports) are open on each one.

nmap is the single most important tool in any ethical hacker's toolkit. It was created in 1997 by Gordon Lyon (aka Fyodor) and has been used in countless security audits since. You've probably even seen it in movies — it appeared in The Matrix Reloaded, Die Hard 4, and Mr. Robot.

When you scan your home network (typically 192.168.1.0/24 or 192.168.0.0/24), nmap sends tiny packets to every possible address in that range and listens for responses. The '/24' means 'check all 256 addresses in this subnet' — from .0 to .255.

For each device it finds, nmap checks common ports (think of ports as numbered doors on a building). Each port runs a specific service: port 80 is HTTP (websites), port 22 is SSH (remote access), port 443 is HTTPS (secure websites), and so on. There are 65,535 possible ports on every device.

nmap reports each port in one of three states:
- **Open**: The port is accepting connections. A service is running and listening. This is what hackers look for.
- **Closed**: The port is accessible but no service is listening. The door exists, but nobody's home.
- **Filtered**: nmap can't tell if the port is open or closed because a firewall is blocking the probe. The door has a bouncer who won't let you peek inside.

A basic scan of your home network will probably reveal your router, phones, smart TVs, gaming consoles, and maybe some IoT devices you forgot about. Many people are shocked to discover how many devices are actually on their network. This is why scanning your own network is a great first step in securing your home — you can't protect what you don't know about.

commands.description: Scan all 256 IP addresses on your home network subnet. This performs a basic host discovery and port scan. You need sudo for some scan types.

Nmap scan report for 192.168.1.1
Host is up (0.0034s latency).
Not shown: 995 closed ports
PORT    STATE SERVICE
22/tcp  open  ssh
53/tcp  open  domain
80/tcp  open  http
443/tcp open  https

Nmap scan report for 192.168.1.105
Host is up (0.012s latency).

PORT   STATE SERVICE
22/tcp open  ssh

Nmap done: 256 IP addresses (4 hosts up) scanned in 12.34 seconds
commands.troubleshooting: If the scan seems slow or returns no results, your subnet might be different. Run 'ip a' or 'ifconfig' first to check your actual IP range. If you're on 192.168.0.x, scan 192.168.0.0/24 instead.
commands.legalNote: Only run this on YOUR home network. Scanning other networks is illegal.

challenge.question: Scan your home network and count how many devices are connected. Which device has the most open ports? What services are running on those ports?
challenge.hint: Use 'sudo nmap 192.168.1.0/24' (adjust the subnet if yours is different). Look at the summary line at the bottom that says 'X hosts up'. For the device with the most ports, check each scan report section.
challenge.answer: Results will vary per network. Your router (usually .1) typically has the most open ports (SSH, DNS, HTTP, HTTPS). Count the 'Host is up' entries for total devices. Common surprises: smart TVs with open ports, forgotten IoT devices, or neighbors' devices if your WiFi password is weak.

realWorld: In 2017, a 14-year-old student in the UK was visited by police after running nmap scans on his school's network from a classroom computer. Even though he didn't access any data, the school reported it as a 'hacking attempt.' The incident is a reminder: even simple reconnaissance tools like nmap can land you in serious trouble if used on networks you don't own. The student faced disciplinary action and a police warning.
funFact: nmap can scan the entire internet (all 4.3 billion IPv4 addresses) in under 45 minutes using its sibling tool 'masscan'. Researchers have done this to map every publicly accessible device on Earth — and found millions of devices with zero security, including baby monitors, traffic lights, and power plant controls.
